Each ensemble here is a uniform sample, drawn with `sample_communities`, from a
`FeasibleCommunities` polytope: the interaction strengths, self-regulation and growth rates
that make a given biomass vector `x` an equilibrium of Lotka–Volterra dynamics on a given web.
The growth rates are coordinates, basal rates in `[0, 5]` and consumer rates in `[-1, 0]`, every
species may self-regulate, and every magnitude is in `[0, 5]`. The stable fraction is the share
of sampled community matrices `J = diag(x) A` whose eigenvalues all have negative real part.
Rebuild with `just gallery`.

Biomasses are divided by their geometric mean before sampling. The equilibrium rows divide the
growth rates by biomasses, so the scale of `x` against the rate intervals and the bounds changes
the polytope.

```{julia}
using FoodWebs, CairoMakie, PolytopeSamplers
using Distributions: Uniform
using LinearAlgebra: eigvals
using Random: Xoshiro
using Statistics: mean, quantile
using Printf: @sprintf
using Markdown: Markdown

geometric_unit(x) = x ./ exp(mean(log.(x)))
stable(J) = maximum(real, eigvals(J)) < 0
stable_fraction(res) = mean(c -> stable(c.J), res.communities)
nothing
```

## Generated pyramids

Five generalized cascade webs with 15 species and connectance 0.15 get the biomasses
`x = ρ^(level - 1)`, with `level` the trophic level, so that `ρ` is the biomass ratio per
trophic level: `ρ < 1` is an Eltonian pyramid and `ρ > 1` an inverted one. Each web and ratio is
sampled twice, with the gain on each link at most its loss (efficiency cap 1) and at most 0.3
of it (cap 0.3). The dashed line is the stable fraction of `random_predprey` matrices on the
same webs, with magnitudes from `Uniform(0, 1)`, conversion efficiency 0.3 and diagonal `-1`,
which impose no equilibrium; their self-regulation dominates and every one is stable.

```{julia}
webs = [generalized_cascade_network(Xoshiro(10 + k), 15, 0.15; basal_paths = true) for k in 1:5]
ratios = exp.(range(log(0.2), log(5.0); length = 9))
caps = (1.0, 0.3)
sweep = Dict(
    (cap, k, ρ) => let x = geometric_unit(ρ .^ (trophic_levels(web) .- 1))
        fc = FeasibleCommunities(web, x; efficiency = (0.0, cap), bounds = (0.0, 5.0))
        sample_communities(Xoshiro(k), fc; target_ess = 300)
    end
    for cap in caps for (k, web) in enumerate(webs) for ρ in ratios
)
baseline = [mean(stable(random_predprey(Xoshiro(100 + k), web, Uniform(0, 1), 0.3)) for _ in 1:1000) for (k, web) in enumerate(webs)]
@assert all(res.converged for res in values(sweep))
nothing
```

```{julia}
fig = Figure(size = (800, 450))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "biomass ratio per trophic level ρ", ylabel = "stable fraction",
    xticks = [0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5])
colors = Makie.wong_colors()
for (c, cap) in enumerate(caps)
    for k in eachindex(webs)
        lines!(ax, ratios, [stable_fraction(sweep[(cap, k, ρ)]) for ρ in ratios]; color = (colors[c], 0.3))
    end
    lines!(ax, ratios, [mean(stable_fraction(sweep[(cap, k, ρ)]) for k in eachindex(webs)) for ρ in ratios];
        color = colors[c], linewidth = 3, label = "feasible, efficiency cap $cap")
end
hlines!(ax, [mean(baseline)]; color = :gray, linestyle = :dash, label = @sprintf("random_predprey, %.3f", mean(baseline)))
vlines!(ax, [1.0]; color = :black, linewidth = 0.5)
axislegend(ax; position = :lb)
ylims!(ax, 0, 1.03)
fig
```

The thin lines are single webs and the thick lines their mean. The stable fractions have a Monte
Carlo standard error of about 0.03 at an effective sample size of 300. With the gain free up to
the loss, the stable fraction stays near 0.95 at every ratio. With the cap at 0.3 it falls from
about 0.9 at `ρ = 0.2` to about 0.7 at `ρ = 5`, most of the fall coming before `ρ = 1`, and
varies between webs by up to 0.3.

### Spectral geometry

The eigenvalues of every tenth sampled matrix, for one web under the efficiency cap 0.3, for an
Eltonian and an inverted pyramid. The inverted pyramid shrinks the eigenvalues towards the origin
(note the axis scales), and the unstable matrices have a real eigenvalue just above zero:

```{julia}
fig = Figure(size = (900, 450))
for (k, ρ) in enumerate((ratios[1], ratios[end]))
    res = sweep[(0.3, 1, ρ)]
    λ = reduce(vcat, eigvals(c.J) for c in res.communities[1:10:end])
    ax = Axis(fig[1, k]; title = @sprintf("ρ = %.2f, stable fraction %.2f", ρ, stable_fraction(res)),
        xlabel = "Re λ", ylabel = "Im λ")
    scatter!(ax, real.(λ), imag.(λ); markersize = 3, color = (:black, 0.3))
    vlines!(ax, [0.0]; color = :red, linestyle = :dash)
end
fig
```

```{julia}
rows = map((ratios[1], ratios[5], ratios[end])) do ρ
    res = sweep[(0.3, 1, ρ)]
    abscissa = [maximum(real, eigvals(c.J)) for c in res.communities]
    spread = [maximum(abs ∘ imag, eigvals(c.J)) for c in res.communities]
    @sprintf("| %.2f | %.3f | %.3f | %.3f |", ρ, quantile(abscissa, 0.5), quantile(abscissa, 0.9), quantile(spread, 0.5))
end
Markdown.parse(join(["| ρ | median max Re λ | 90% max Re λ | median max abs(Im λ) |", "|---|---|---|---|", rows...], "\n"))
```

## Observed biomasses

TL84 and TL86 (Tuesday Lake, in the cheddar data) have a body mass and numerical abundance for
every species, so `biomass(fw)` gives an observed biomass vector. Each web is sampled with its
observed biomasses and with the steady-state biomasses from `steady_state_biomass` (transfer
efficiency 0.1, allometric turnover), on the web without cannibalism. The pyramid slope is the
least-squares slope of log biomass against trophic level, `log ρ`.

```{julia}
cheddar = map(["cheddar/tl84", "cheddar/tl86"]) do name
    fw = foodweb(name)
    web, _ = remove_cannibalism(fw)
    sets = (
        observed = geometric_unit(Float64.(biomass(fw))),
        steady_state = geometric_unit(steady_state_biomass(fw; efficiency = 0.1, turnover = :allometric)),
    )
    map(collect(pairs(sets))) do (label, x)
        fractions = map(caps) do cap
            fc = FeasibleCommunities(web, x; efficiency = (0.0, cap), bounds = (0.0, 5.0))
            stable_fraction(sample_communities(Xoshiro(7), fc; target_ess = 200))
        end
        (; name = fw.name, label, slope = pyramid_slope(web, x), dimension = dimension(FeasibleCommunities(web, x)), fractions)
    end
end
rows = [@sprintf("| %s | %s | %.2f | %d | %.2f | %.2f |", r.name, r.label, r.slope, r.dimension, r.fractions...) for r in reduce(vcat, cheddar)]
Markdown.parse(join(["| web | biomass | pyramid slope | dimension | stable, cap 1 | stable, cap 0.3 |", "|---|---|---|---|---|---|", rows...], "\n"))
```

The observed Tuesday Lake pyramids are top-heavy (positive slope), and the steady-state pyramids
from the same webs are Eltonian. These webs have over 500 dimensions, so each stable fraction
comes from 200 effective samples, with a standard error of about 0.035. The pyramid shape has no
consistent effect across the two webs. Under the cap 0.3 the observed TL84 biomasses are more
stable than the steady-state ones (0.58 against 0.42), and under the cap 1 less stable (0.38
against 0.58); TL86 differs little between its two biomass vectors under either cap.
